title: Todoist vs Notion in 2026: Which To-Do App Wins?
body_md:
![todoist.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/1.png)
*Screenshot of todoist.com ([source](https://www.todoist.com/pricing))*

**Short answer:** If you want a fast, reliable place to capture and finish tasks, pick Todoist. If your tasks are tangled up with notes, docs, project trackers, and a team wiki, pick Notion. Todoist is the better *to-do app*; Notion is the better *workspace that can hold a to-do list* — and the price gap between them is wider than most people expect.

## Quick Comparison

![todoist.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/2.png)
*Screenshot of todoist.com ([source](https://www.todoist.com/help/articles/todoist-plans-pricing-and-billing-faq-Vq2z0HWL6))*

| Comparison | **Todoist** | **Notion** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free plan** | Beginner: free forever, 5 personal projects, Smart Quick Add, list & board layouts, 3 filters | Free: unlimited blocks solo (limited for 2+ members), 10 guests, 5 MB file uploads, 7-day page history |
| **Entry paid plan** | Pro — $5/mo billed yearly ($60/yr), $7/mo month-to-month | Plus — $10/member/mo billed yearly, $12/mo month-to-month |
| **Team plan** | Business — $8/user/mo yearly ($96/user/yr), $10/user/mo monthly | Business — $20/member/mo yearly, $24/member/mo monthly |
| **Top tier** | None — Business is the ceiling | Enterprise — custom quote |
| **Core strength** | Fast task capture, natural-language dates, recurring tasks, filters | Databases, docs, wikis, custom views, all-in-one workspace |
| **Built-in AI** | AI features on paid plans (Task Assist, Ramble) | Full Notion AI requires the Business tier |
| **Learning curve** | Low — usable in ten minutes | Medium to high — you build your own system |
| **Best for** | Individuals and small teams who want tasks done | Teams that want tasks, docs, and knowledge in one place |

Prices are US dollars, before tax, as listed by each vendor; both companies bill per user/member and discount annual billing.

## Pricing: Todoist Is Roughly Half the Cost

![notion.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/3.png)
*Screenshot of notion.com ([source](https://www.notion.com/pricing))*

Todoist keeps it simple: three plans, Beginner (free), Pro, and Business.Pro runs $5/month billed annually ($60/year) or $7/month billed monthly, and Business is $8/user/month annually ($96/user/year) or $10/user/month monthly. Note that prices went up in December 2025 — Pro rose from $4 to $5 and Business from $6 to $8 on the annual plans — so older articles quoting $4 are out of date.

Notion has four tiers — Free, Plus, Business, and Enterprise — and costs more per seat. Plus is $10 per member per month billed yearly ($12 monthly), Business is $20 billed yearly ($24 monthly), and Enterprise is a custom quote. There's also a metered layer on top: Notion's AI features live on Business, with agent usage priced separately in credits.

Run the math for a five-person team on annual billing and Todoist Business lands at $480/year versus $600/year for Notion Plus — and $1,200/year if that team needs Notion Business. That doesn't make Notion overpriced; it's doing far more than task tracking. But if tasks are all you need, you're paying a premium for capability you won't use.

## Ease of Use: Opinionated vs. Open-Ended

Todoist is opinionated, and that's the point. You type "email Dana about the Q3 deck Friday 9am p1," and it parses the date, time, and priority for you. Smart Quick Add, task reminders, and list and board views are available even on the free Beginner plan. There's essentially no setup phase — you install it and start dumping tasks.

Notion is the opposite: a blank canvas. You manage tasks through Kanban boards, calendar, and list views, track related information on each item, change statuses, collaborate, and work with spreadsheet-style databases.

That flexibility is genuinely powerful, but you're the architect. A Notion task system is something you *design* — properties, filtered views, relations between a tasks database and a projects database — and then maintain. Some people love that. Others spend a weekend building a gorgeous dashboard and never open it again.

A useful gut check: if you've ever abandoned a productivity system because tweaking it became the hobby, Todoist's guardrails are a feature, not a limitation.

## The Feature That Actually Separates Them

Todoist's edge is *capture speed and nudging*. Recurring tasks, natural-language scheduling, priority flags, and saved filters are the everyday machinery of getting things done, and Todoist has spent years polishing them. Pro adds the calendar layout, task duration, custom reminders, 150 filter views, unlimited history, Task Assist, and Deadlines.

Notion's edge is *context*. A task in Notion isn't just a line of text — it's a page that can hold the meeting notes, the spec, the client brief, and a link to the parent project. For knowledge work where "the task" and "the document" are inseparable, that's a real advantage no standalone to-do app can match.

The trade-off shows up in daily friction. Adding a quick task in Notion takes more clicks and more thought about where it belongs, and mobile capture has never been as instant as Todoist's. Conversely, Todoist can't hold your team wiki, and it won't replace a project database with rollups and relations.

## Collaboration and AI

For teams, Todoist's Business plan is deliberately narrow: a shared team workspace, up to 500 team projects, granular activity logs, role-based permissions, centralized billing, and SOC 2 Type II compliance, plus shared templates and up to 1,000 team members and guests. That's a solid shared task layer — not a full project management suite. No Gantt charts, no dependencies.

Notion scales differently. Business adds SAML SSO, private teamspaces, granular database permissions, 90-day page history, and premium connections such as GitHub and Asana syncs, and Enterprise extends page history to unlimited.

AI is where budgets diverge most. Full Notion AI stopped being a $10 add-on in May 2025 and now lives on Business, so you can't bolt it onto a $10 Plus plan. Notion Agent, AI meeting notes, and enterprise search are fully included only from Business up; Free and Plus get a limited trial.

Todoist's AI sits on its far cheaper paid plans, but it's narrower in scope — it helps you phrase, break down, and organize tasks rather than summarize documents or search a knowledge base.

## Who Should Use Which

- **Solo professionals and freelancers tracking personal work:** Todoist. Pro at $60/year is hard to beat, and the free tier is genuinely usable if you stay under five projects.
- **Students and casual list-makers:** Todoist Beginner, free. Notion's free tier also works well if you want notes and tasks together — and eligible students and teachers can get a one-member Plus workspace free.
- **Small teams sharing a task list:** Todoist Business. At $8 per user versus $20, it's 40% of the per-seat cost of Notion Business and requires no system-building.
- **Teams whose work lives in docs, wikis, and trackers:** Notion. Tasks-plus-context in one workspace is worth the extra spend, and it consolidates tools you're probably paying for separately.
- **Teams that want built-in AI over their own content:** Notion Business — just budget the $20/seat honestly, plus credits if you lean on agents.
- **People who've bounced off complex tools before:** Todoist, every time.
- **Honestly? Many people run both:** Notion as the knowledge base, Todoist as the daily action list. The combined cost is still modest, and each tool does what it's actually good at.

## FAQ

**Can Notion fully replace Todoist?**
Functionally, yes — you can build a task database with due dates, priorities, and recurring items. Practically, it depends on whether you'll accept slower capture and weaker reminders in exchange for keeping everything in one place.

**Is Todoist's free plan enough?**
For a lot of people, yes. Beginner is free, with 5 personal projects, list and board layouts, task reminders, 3 custom filters and 1 week of activity history. The project cap is the usual reason to upgrade.

**Which is cheaper for a 10-person team?**
Todoist, clearly. Business runs $96 per user per year on annual billing — $960 for ten seats — while ten people on Notion is $1,200 a year on Plus and $2,400 on Business.

**Do I have to pay annually to get the advertised price?**
Effectively, yes. The headline "$5" and "$8" Todoist figures are annual-billed rates; monthly billing is 40% more on Pro and 25% more on Business. Notion's pricing page shows $10 and $20 by default under its "Pay yearly" toggle, so flip it before you commit a budget line.

*Updated October 2026. This comparison is based on each vendor's published pricing and documentation plus public reports, not a hands-on test; confirm current prices before you buy.*

## My Take

I think Todoist wins this matchup for most people asking the question in the first place, and the reason is narrow: the thing that kills to-do systems is friction at capture, and Todoist has less of it than anything Notion can be configured into. If a task takes four seconds to log, you log it. If it takes thirty, you don't, and then the system is a lie.

My read on the pricing is that the gap is the real story, not the feature lists. Notion moved full AI behind Business in 2025, which means the honest comparison for an AI-curious team is $8/user versus $20/member — Todoist at 40% of the cost. If you're buying Notion for AI you don't end up using, that's a bad trade.

The fair point for Notion: tasks that are really documents belong in a document tool. A client project with a brief, a spec, and a status field is genuinely worse off as a one-line Todoist entry with a comment thread. Teams doing that kind of work should pay the premium and stop shopping.

What I'd watch is Todoist's post-December-2025 pricing. A 25% Pro increase and a 33% Business increase in one move suggests the cheap-forever era is over, and a legacy plan won't protect you from the next one. Price the two-year total, not the monthly line.

And I'm not a financial advisor — if this is a budget line for a real company, run the per-seat math against your actual headcount rather than the five- and ten-person examples above.
